---
title: "Metadata for Reuse"

---

A data file is not necessarily usable just because it opens. **Metadata** (information about the data) provide the context needed to interpret, evaluate, reuse, and share the data correctly. In this LilyPad, you'll discover which metadata you need by trying to use a dataset without them.

## 1. Data Usability

[<i class="bi bi-clock" aria-hidden="true"></i> About 15 minutes]{.pond-pad-time}

Imagine that you work for a city office that checks whether schools meet lead (Pb) exposure standards. A testing company has just sampled the soil in the playground at MADISON ELEM., and a colleague forwards you their file:

> Here's the soil data from Madison. Can you tell me whether the playground is above the 400 ppm limit for children's play areas?

(ppm means *parts per million*: 400 ppm is 400 milligrams of lead per kilogram of soil.)

This is the file, `madison_soil.csv`, exactly as you received it:

::: {.pond-pad-notes}
```
id,loc,d,Pb,m,f
M-01,road,1,610,12,1
M-02,road,6,380,15,1
M-03,road,15,99,18,0
M-04,sandbox,1,99,10,1
M-05,sandbox,6,70,14,1
M-06,wall,1,360,20,1
M-07,wall,6,730,22,0
```
:::

[Fictional school, company and values, created for The Pond (2026).]{.pond-pad-credit}

It opens without any trouble. Let's see whether you can use it.

### 1.1 Where did this file come from?

Before you start, think about the file itself. **What would you want to know about where it came from?** Select as many as you like, then reveal our answer.

<!--
"What would you need?" activities. Each option becomes a button; data-needed="true" marks
the options that are needed. The .pond-md-meta div is the metadata revealed at the end.
Without JavaScript, everything is shown as text.
-->

::: {#pond-md-need-source .pond-md-need}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Who collected the samples" data-needed="true"}
A company you know, a student project, or an unknown source? Knowing who did the work offers clue as to their likely practices and conventions (though not always!).
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Which school, where, and when" data-needed="true"}
Is this really MADISON ELEM., and this year's sampling? The file names no school and no date.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Where the file was obtained" data-needed="true"}
From the company itself, or from somewhere else? An original from the source is easier to check than a copy of a copy.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Whether anyone changed it" data-needed="true"}
Was anything removed, renamed, or recalculated before it reached you?
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The file size"}
Irrelevant: the file size tells you nothing about where the data came from.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The software used to open it"}
Irrelevant: any spreadsheet or text editor opens a CSV (comma-separated values) file the same way.
:::

::: {.pond-md-meta}
**What your colleague tells you:** The samples were collected at MADISON ELEM. on October 14, 2026, by the field crew of Northgate Soil Testing, a company that the city has a contract with. Your colleague downloaded the file from the company's client portal and didn't change it.
:::
:::

This information about where data came from, and what happened to them along the way, is called **provenance**. It doesn't make the data trustworthy on its own, but it gives you what you need to *evaluate* the data. You'll look at provenance in more depth in [Data Quality and Provenance](../data-quality/index.qmd).

#### Key takeaway 1.1

Before using a dataset, find out who produced it, where you got it, and whether anything changed along the way. This provenance doesn't make data trustworthy, but without it you can't judge whether they are.

### 1.2 How deep is each sample?

Lead tends to build up near the surface, which is also the soil that children touch. So depth matters.

**Your turn!** Which column do you think contains the depth?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad-whatif" role="group" aria-label="Which column contains the depth?">
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="A reasonable guess: d might stand for depth. But m might stand for meters…">d</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Possible: m might stand for meters. But d might stand for depth…">m</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Fair enough: from the file alone, you can't be sure.">I can't tell</button>
</div>
<p class="pond-pad-take" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
```

Now **assume that `d` is the depth.** How deep is sample M-02, in meters?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad">
  <label for="pond-md-depth"><strong>Depth of M-02, in meters</strong></label>
  <div class="pond-pad-row">
    <input id="pond-md-depth" class="form-control pond-md-save" type="number" step="any" placeholder="e.g. 0.5">
  </div>
</div>
```

You can type a number, but can you be sure it's right? **What would you need to know?**

::: {#pond-md-need-depth .pond-md-need}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Which column is the depth" data-needed="true"}
The column names (`d`, `m`) are too short to be sure.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The units of depth" data-needed="true"}
Is 6 a depth in millimeters, centimeters, inches, or feet? Each gives a very different sample.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Where depth is measured from" data-needed="true"}
From the ground surface, or from the top of a layer of mulch or sand? To the top, middle, or bottom of the sample?
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The instrument used"}
Not a first choice: the type of lead analyzer says little about how depth was recorded.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The time of sampling"}
Irrelevant here: the time of day doesn't change how deep a sample was.
:::

::: {.pond-md-meta}
**You ask the testing company, which replies:** `d` is the depth below the ground surface to the middle of the sample, **in inches**.
:::
:::

::: {#pond-md-depth-check .pond-pad data-after="pond-md-need-depth"}
```{=html}
<button type="button" class="btn btn-primary" id="pond-md-depth-btn">Check my answer</button>
<p class="pond-pad-take" id="pond-md-depth-out" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
```
:::

#### Key takeaway 1.2

Raw values are unusable without ancillary information, known as metadata. When you archive your data, make sure you include all the information necessary to use them, from the standpoint of a reasonable person who does not live in your head.

### 1.3 Missing Values

Before you average anything, you need to remove the missing values: samples for which there is no lead measurement.

**Your turn!** Drop the rows that you think have no lead measurement, and watch the average change.

::: {#pond-md-drop .pond-pad-notes .pond-pad-wide}
| id | loc | d | Pb | m | f |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| M-01 | road | 1 | 610 | 12 | 1 |
| M-02 | road | 6 | 380 | 15 | 1 |
| M-03 | road | 15 | 99 | 18 | 0 |
| M-04 | sandbox | 1 | 99 | 10 | 1 |
| M-05 | sandbox | 6 | 70 | 14 | 1 |
| M-06 | wall | 1 | 360 | 20 | 1 |
| M-07 | wall | 6 | 730 | 22 | 0 |
:::

Did you drop any? Nothing in the file says that a value is missing. **What would you need to know?**

::: {#pond-md-need-missing .pond-md-need}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="How missing values are recorded" data-needed="true"}
Some files leave a blank, others use a special code such as `-999` or `99`.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Why a value is missing" data-needed="true"}
Not analyzed? Sample lost? Below what the instrument can detect? Each has different implications.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The highest value lead can reach"}
Irrelevant: lead in soil can range from a few ppm to many thousands. No value in this file is impossible.
:::

::: {.pond-md-meta}
**You ask the testing company, which replies:** a lead value of **99** means that the sample was *not analyzed*. That's **M-03** only: lead at **M-04** was measured, and really is 99 ppm.

Here is what each choice does to the average of all the samples:

| Your choice | Average lead | Compared with the 400 ppm limit |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| Keep every row (the raw average) | 335 ppm | Below |
| Drop M-03 only (correct) | 375 ppm | Below |
| Drop both 99s | 430 ppm | **Above** |

This is a consequential number. An average above 400 ppm could close the playground, alarm parents, and trigger an expensive cleanup. Here, deleting one real measurement, because an undocumented code looked like it, would have done exactly that. (This isn't the final answer yet: quality control and dry soil will change the picture again in 1.4 and 1.5.)
:::
:::

Lead at 99 ppm is a perfectly ordinary value, so `99` was a particularly unwise choice to encode missingness: nothing in the numbers can tell the two rows apart: only the metadata can.

#### What should `99` have been?

**Your turn!** Pick the best way to record "no value here," then reveal our take on each option.

::: {#pond-md-need-code .pond-md-need data-yes="Recommended" data-no="Problematic" data-button="Reveal our take"}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="0"}
The worst choice: 0 is a real and reassuring value ("no lead at all"). A sample that was never analyzed would look like the cleanest soil in the playground.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="-999"}
Impossible for a concentration, so a person would spot it. But software doesn't know that: unless told otherwise, it averages −999 in with the real values, so that an average of a 1000 with this -999 would come out close to 0: a very troublesome _false negative_. 
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="An empty cell"}
Ambiguous: was the value not measured, forgotten, or deleted by accident? Software also disagrees: some tools skip empty cells, others treat them as 0.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="NA"}
Short for "not available." It's widely used, but it's just text: whether it's read as "missing" depends on the software.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="NaN" data-needed="true"}
"Not a number," a special value defined by the [IEEE 754 standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754) for how computers do arithmetic. Nearly all numerical software recognizes it, and it can never be mistaken for a measurement. Arithmetic with NaN gives NaN (1 + NaN = NaN), so a missing value can't sneak into a calculation as a number: tools either skip it or tell you it's there. 
:::
:::

::: {.pond-pad data-after="pond-md-need-code"}
<details class="pond-pad-reveal">
<summary>NaN isn't perfect either</summary>

- **In a CSV file, `NaN` is just three letters.** Python's pandas and R read it as a number; a spreadsheet may show it as text.
- **NaN is not equal to anything, including itself.** A test such as `x == NaN` is always false, so software provides dedicated checks (`isnan`, `is.nan`).
- Not all analysis code can deal with NaNs. For instance, trying to estimate the naive average of all these measurements would produce a NaN. However, most software worth its salt can handle that (e.g. [NumPy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.nanmean.html)). 
- **It doesn't say *why* the value is missing.** Not analyzed, sample lost, failed quality control, withheld for privacy: each might call for a different decision. Record the reason in a separate column, and say what it means in the metadata.

Also, not every gap is missing data. A lab may report `<10`: lead is **below the detection limit** of 10 ppm, the lowest level its instrument can measure reliably. That's information (the value is less than 10 ppm), and replacing it with NaN would throw it away.

</details>
:::

#### Key takeaway 1.3

Even a simple [data cleaning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_cleansing) step such as removing missing values hinges on metadata. Before you share data, record missing values in a way that can't be mistaken for a measurement (such as NaN), flag *why* a value is reported missing, and document both conventions. 

### 1.4 Quality Control

Testing companies check their measurements before releasing them. This is called **quality control** (QC). The column `f` looks like a QC flag.

**Your turn!** To keep only the measurements that passed QC, which rows would you keep?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad-whatif" role="group" aria-label="Which rows passed quality control?">
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Many datasets do use 0 for &quot;no problem&quot;… but many others use 1 for &quot;passed.&quot;">Rows where f = 0</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Many datasets do use 1 for &quot;passed&quot;… but many others use 0 for &quot;no problem.&quot;">Rows where f = 1</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Right: the numbers 0 and 1 mean nothing until someone says what they stand for.">I can't tell</button>
</div>
<p class="pond-pad-take" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
```

**What would you need to know?**

::: {#pond-md-need-qc .pond-md-need}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="What each flag value means" data-needed="true"}
Does 1 mean "passed" or "problem"? Conventions differ between companies and fields.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Why a measurement failed"}
Useful to know, but not needed to filter the table: the decision has already been made.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The average of the f column"}
Irrelevant: the average of a set of codes means nothing.
:::

::: {.pond-md-meta}
**You ask the testing company, which replies:** `f` is the QC flag **for lead only**: **1 = passed**, 0 = failed. Depth and moisture are not flagged.

So you keep M-01, M-02, M-04, M-05 and M-06. M-07's 730 ppm, the highest value in the file, failed QC. M-03 failed too: it was never analyzed.
:::
:::

Metadata can be specific to a single variable: here the flag tells you about lead, not about the rest of the row. In [Different Types of Data](../data-type/index.qmd), you met a similar QC/status column; there, its meaning was written out in words.

#### Key takeaway 1.4

Codes such as 0 and 1 mean nothing on their own. The metadata must say what each value stands for, and which variable it applies to.

### 1.5 Dry soil, or wet soil?

Look back at how we defined ppm at the start: "400 milligrams of lead per kilogram of soil." We left out a consequential detail: the limit applies to lead per kilogram of **dry** soil.

**Your turn!** Which of the surface samples (`d` = 1) are above the 400 ppm limit?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad-choices" id="pond-md-surface" role="group" aria-label="Surface samples above 400 ppm">
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-id="M-01">M-01 (road, 610)</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-id="M-04">M-04 (sandbox, 99)</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-id="M-06">M-06 (wall, 360)</button>
</div>
```

This one requires knowledge specific to soil science. **What would you need to know?**

::: {#pond-md-need-dry .pond-md-need}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Whether Pb is per dry or wet soil" data-needed="true"}
Labs can report lead per kilogram of soil *as received* (water included) or per kilogram of *dried* soil. Wet soil is partly water, so the same soil gives a lower number when measured wet.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="What m means" data-needed="true"}
If `m` is the water content, you can use it to convert from wet to dry soil. But as a percentage of what?
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The weather on the day"}
Rain may explain *why* the soil was wet, but you need the measured water content, not the weather.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The technician's name"}
Irrelevant: it doesn't change what the numbers mean.
:::

::: {.pond-md-meta}
**You ask the testing company, which replies:** lead (`Pb`) is measured in ppm on soil **as received**, without drying. `m` is the water content, as a **percentage of the wet sample's mass**.

So lead per kilogram of dry soil is `Pb / (1 − m/100)`:

| id | loc | Pb, as received | m | Pb, dry soil |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| M-01 | road | 610 | 12 | **693** |
| M-04 | sandbox | 99 | 10 | 110 |
| M-06 | wall | 360 | 20 | **450** |

M-01 *and* M-06 are above 400 ppm.
:::
:::

::: {#pond-md-surface-out .pond-pad data-after="pond-md-need-dry"}
:::

This is the kind of metadata that a generic checklist ("include units") would never catch: the units were ppm all along. Each discipline has its own definitions that change what a number means. In [Data Quality and Provenance](../data-quality/index.qmd), you'll see how preparing a sample (drying, sieving) affects the measurement itself.

#### Key takeaway 1.5

Some metadata are specific to a discipline, like whether lead was measured in wet or dry soil. No generic checklist will catch them: ask yourself what a specialist in your field would need to know to use your numbers. 

### 1.6 Can you share it?

You now have a clean dataset. Your office wants to post it in a public data repository, and to include it in a report to denizens of the town.

**Your turn!** Are you allowed to?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad-whatif" role="group" aria-label="Are you allowed to share the data?">
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="The city paid for the sampling, so it seems fair… but paying for a service doesn't always mean owning the data. It depends on the contract.">Yes</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="That's the cautious answer, but nothing in the file says you can't, either.">No</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Right: nothing in the file says.">I can't tell</button>
</div>
<p class="pond-pad-take" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
```

**What would you need to know?**

::: {#pond-md-need-share .pond-md-need}
::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The license" data-needed="true"}
A **license** states what others may do with the data: copy, modify, redistribute, and under what conditions (for instance, whether they must credit the creators).
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="The contract, or other terms of use" data-needed="true"}
A contract, a privacy rule, or a data use agreement can restrict sharing, or require it. Here, the city's contract decides which license applies.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Whether you can download the file"}
Irrelevant: you already have it. Having access to data is not the same as having permission to share them.
:::

::: {.pond-md-option data-name="Whether your colleague says it's fine"}
Not enough: an informal "go ahead" is easily forgotten or misremembered, and may not be your colleague's to give.
:::

::: {.pond-md-meta}
**The file says nothing**, so you can't assume you're allowed. Your office checks the city's contract with Northgate Soil Testing: it requires all data delivered to the city to be released under an open license. Northgate adds the license to the dataset's metadata:

**License:** [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) (public domain). Anyone may copy, adapt, and share the data, for any purpose, without asking permission.

CC0 asks nothing in return, not even credit. But scientific practice still expects you to cite the data you use: see [Citing Data](../citing-data/index.qmd).

Requiring open licenses is common for publicly funded data. In the United States, federal guidance on [open licenses](https://resources.data.gov/open-licenses/) asks agencies to make sure that data they obtain through contracts aren't locked behind restrictive licenses, and encourages them to use CC0.
:::
:::

Permission should be written into the metadata, not left to an email or a hallway conversation, so that it travels with the data. You'll put this into practice in [Preparing Data for Sharing](../sharing-data/index.qmd). To learn how licenses work, and how to choose one for your own data, dive into [Licensing](../../../deep-water/licensing/index.qmd) in the Deep End.

#### Key takeaway 1.6

Having data is not the same as being allowed to share them. State the license and any reuse conditions in the metadata, so that permission travels with the data.

### So, is the playground above 400 ppm?

<details class="pond-pad-reveal pond-md-recap">
<summary>Compare the file as received with what the metadata told you</summary>

| | From the file alone | With the metadata |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Depth of M-02 | 6 *somethings* | 6 inches, or 0.15 m |
| Missing values | None visible, or both 99s | M-03 only |
| Rows that passed QC | Your guess | M-01, M-02, M-04, M-05, M-06 |
| Surface samples above 400 ppm | M-01 (610) | M-01 (693) and M-06 (450), in dry soil |
| Can you share the data? | Unknown | Yes, without conditions (CC0), though you should still cite it |

With the metadata, two of the three surface spots are above the limit. Without them, you would have reported one. Whether three spots are enough to judge the whole playground is a question about data *quality*, which you'll explore in [Data Quality and Provenance](../data-quality/index.qmd).

</details>

### Key takeaway 1

At every step, the file opened fine and the numbers looked ordinary. What stopped you was missing *context*: where the data came from, what each column means, how missing values and QC are coded, what a measurement is relative to, and what you are allowed to do with the data.

## 2. What metadata did you actually need?

[<i class="bi bi-clock" aria-hidden="true"></i> About 4 minutes]{.pond-pad-time}

**Your turn!** Think back over the exercise. What information did you need in order to trust, interpret, clean, use, and share the data?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad">
  <label for="pond-md-reflect"><strong>The information I needed</strong></label>
  <textarea id="pond-md-reflect" class="pond-pad-response pond-md-save" rows="5"
    placeholder="List what you needed, and for which step..."></textarea>
</div>
```

<details class="pond-pad-reveal">
<summary>Compare with our answer</summary>

Metadata are often grouped into two broad kinds:

::: {.grid}
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-body}
#### Scientific metadata

Help you understand and evaluate the science:

- variable names and definitions (`d`, `m`)
- units (inches, ppm)
- missing-value conventions (`99`)
- QC definitions (`f`: 1 = passed, lead only)
- domain-specific definitions (as received vs. dry soil)
- methods and calibration
- where and when the samples were taken
- uncertainty
- **provenance**: who collected the data, and what happened to them
:::
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-body}
#### Administrative metadata

Help you identify, manage, access, and reuse the dataset:

- creator and contributors (Northgate Soil Testing)
- institution (the city)
- identifier (a name or number that points to this dataset)
- contact information
- license (CC0, as required by the city's contract)
- access restrictions
- reuse and redistribution conditions
- **provenance**: where the file was obtained, and who is responsible for it
:::
:::
:::
:::

These categories are not rigid. Provenance appears in both: it helps you interpret the science, *and* it tells you who is responsible for the data.

</details>

### Key takeaway 2

> Metadata serve different purposes. Some help researchers understand and evaluate the science, while others help identify, manage, access, and reuse the dataset.

## 3. From unstructured to structured metadata

[<i class="bi bi-clock" aria-hidden="true"></i> About 6 minutes]{.pond-pad-time}

### 3.1 Organize the metadata

Suppose that, instead of answering questions one at a time, Northgate Soil Testing had sent all of its metadata in an email:

::: {.pond-pad-notes}
Soil samples were collected at the MADISON ELEM. playground on October 14, 2026, by our field crew. Depth (d) is the depth below the ground surface to the middle of each sample, in inches. Lead (Pb) is in ppm, measured on the soil as received, without drying; m is the water content, as a percentage of the wet sample's mass. A lead value of 99 means the sample was not analyzed. The flag f applies to lead only: 1 means the measurement passed quality control, 0 that it failed. As required by our contract with the city, the data are released under a CC0 license.
:::

Everything is there, but finding one piece of information means reading the whole paragraph, and a computer can't easily check it.

**Your turn!** Organize this information into a structured form: a table, a list of labeled fields, or anything else you like. There is no single correct structure.

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad">
  <label for="pond-md-structure"><strong>My structured metadata</strong></label>
  <textarea id="pond-md-structure" class="pond-pad-response pond-pad-code pond-md-save" rows="10"
    placeholder="For example:&#10;depth: ..."></textarea>
</div>
```

### 3.2 Same information, different structures

Here is how three other people organized the same paragraph:

::: {.grid}
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-4}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-body}
#### Person A

| variable | units | missing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| d | inches | — |
| Pb | ppm (wet) | 99 |
| m | % | — |
:::
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-4}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-body}
#### Person B

```
depth_unit: in
lead_units: ppm
lead_basis: as received
lead_missing: 99
qc_good: 1
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-4}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-body}
#### Person C

```
d:
  unit: inch
Pb:
  units: mg/kg
  dry: no
  missingValue: 99
  qcFlag: f (1 = pass)
```
:::
:::
:::
:::

**Your turn!** All three are structured. Could a computer combine them automatically?

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad-whatif" role="group" aria-label="Could a computer combine them automatically?">
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Look again: depth_unit, unit and units are three names for the same idea, and in, inch and inches are three spellings of the same unit. A computer can't know they match unless someone tells it.">Yes</button>
  <button type="button" class="pond-pad-tag" aria-pressed="false" data-verdict="Right. depth_unit, unit and units are three names for the same idea; in, inch and inches are three spellings of one unit; ppm and mg/kg are the same unit under two names; and Person A packed two facts into one value, &quot;ppm (wet)&quot;. Structure alone isn't enough.">No</button>
</div>
<p class="pond-pad-take" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
```

### 3.3 Conventions

Structured metadata are easier to find, read, and check than a paragraph. But structure alone doesn't make them **interoperable**, meaning that metadata from different people and programs can work together. For that, a community needs to agree on:

- **field names**: always `units`, never `unit` or `depth_unit`
- **required and optional fields**: e.g. every dataset must have a license
- **definitions**: what exactly each field means
- **allowed values and vocabularies**: e.g. an agreed list of unit spellings, or of terms for "lead in soil"
- **standard representations**: e.g. how to write a date, or a missing value

Such agreements are called **conventions** (or *standards*). Here is Person C's metadata, rewritten in the style of one such convention:

```
Pb:
  long_name: lead in soil, as received
  units: mg kg-1
  ancillary_variables: f
f:
  flag_values: 0, 1
  flag_meanings: failed passed
```

The field names (`long_name`, `units`, `flag_values`, `flag_meanings`) aren't anyone's personal choice: they come from the convention, so any software that follows it knows how to read them.

You don't need to learn any particular convention for this LilyPad. If you're curious, here are a few examples:

- [CF Conventions](https://cfconventions.org/): for climate and environmental data in netCDF files (the example above is in their style).
- [DataCite Metadata Schema](https://schema.datacite.org/): administrative metadata for citing datasets in any field.
- [PaST Thesaurus](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/paleoclimatology/paleoenvironmental-standard-terms-thesaurus): a controlled vocabulary for describing paleoclimate measurements.

### Key takeaway 3

> Structured metadata are useful, but structure alone does not guarantee interoperability. Communities also need agreement about field names, definitions, allowed values, and vocabularies.

---

Now that you understand what the MADISON ELEM. dataset contains, a new question arises: **is it good enough for your purpose?** That's the subject of the next LilyPad, [Data Quality and Provenance](../data-quality/index.qmd).

```{=html}
<div class="pond-pad">
  <p>Keep a record of your answers, side by side with ours, the metadata you uncovered, and the key takeaways.</p>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-primary" id="pond-md-download">Download response summary</button>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<script src="../../../scripts/response-summary.js"></script>
<script src="../../../scripts/pond-activities.js"></script>
<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
  // Learner answers stay in this browser only (shared widgets in scripts/pond-activities.js)
  const state = Pond.store("pond-metadata");
  const { saved, save, hooks } = state;
  ["dropped", "surface"].forEach(k => { if (!Array.isArray(saved[k])) saved[k] = []; });
  Pond.textBoxes(state);
  Pond.whatifs(state);
  const needs = Pond.needBanks(state);

  // 1.2 What does the learner's depth answer imply?
  function depthMessage(v) {
    const near = (a, b) => Math.abs(a - b) <= 0.03 * b;
    if (Number.isNaN(v)) return "Enter a number above first.";
    if (near(v, 0.1524)) return "✓ Right: 6 inches × 0.0254 m per inch = 0.15 m.";
    if (near(v, 0.06)) return "You assumed centimeters (6 cm = 0.06 m). In inches, M-02 is 0.15 m deep: about 2.5 times deeper.";
    if (near(v, 0.006)) return "You assumed millimeters (6 mm = 0.006 m). In inches, M-02 is 0.15 m deep: 25 times deeper.";
    if (near(v, 1.83)) return "You assumed feet (6 ft = 1.83 m). In inches, M-02 is 0.15 m deep.";
    if (near(v, 6)) return "You assumed meters. In inches, M-02 is 0.15 m deep: 40 times shallower.";
    return "Not quite. 6 inches × 0.0254 m per inch = 0.15 m.";
  }
  const depthOut = document.getElementById("pond-md-depth-out");
  document.getElementById("pond-md-depth-btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
    depthOut.textContent = depthMessage(parseFloat(document.getElementById("pond-md-depth").value));
    depthOut.hidden = false;
  });

  // 1.3 Drop rows and watch the average lead change
  const dropBox = document.getElementById("pond-md-drop");
  const dropTable = dropBox.querySelector("table");
  const headers = [...dropTable.querySelectorAll("thead th")].map(th => th.textContent.trim());
  const pbCol = headers.indexOf("Pb");
  dropTable.querySelector("thead tr").insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "<th>Keep?</th>");
  const dropRows = [...dropTable.querySelectorAll("tbody tr")];
  const dropStatus = document.createElement("p");
  dropStatus.className = "pond-pad-status";
  dropStatus.setAttribute("aria-live", "polite");
  dropBox.after(dropStatus);
  const average = rows => Math.round(rows.reduce((a, tr) => a + Number(tr.cells[pbCol].textContent), 0) / rows.length);
  const vsLimit = v => v > 400 ? "<strong>above</strong> the 400 ppm limit" : "below the 400 ppm limit";
  function updateAverage() {
    const kept = dropRows.filter(tr => !saved.dropped.includes(tr.cells[0].textContent.trim()));
    const raw = average(dropRows);
    let html = `Raw average (all ${dropRows.length} rows): ${raw} ppm, ${vsLimit(raw)}.<br>`;
    if (!kept.length) html += "Your cleaned average: you dropped every row.";
    else {
      const mine = average(kept);
      html += `Your cleaned average (${kept.length} rows): <strong>${mine} ppm</strong>, ${vsLimit(mine)}.`;
    }
    dropStatus.innerHTML = html;
  }
  dropRows.forEach(tr => {
    const id = tr.cells[0].textContent.trim();
    const td = document.createElement("td");
    const btn = document.createElement("button");
    btn.type = "button";
    btn.className = "pond-pad-tag pond-pad-small";
    td.append(btn);
    tr.append(td);
    function draw() {
      const dropped = saved.dropped.includes(id);
      tr.classList.toggle("is-dropped", dropped);
      btn.textContent = dropped ? "Dropped" : "Kept";
      btn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(dropped));
      btn.setAttribute("aria-label", `Drop ${id}`);
    }
    btn.addEventListener("click", () => {
      saved.dropped = saved.dropped.includes(id) ? saved.dropped.filter(x => x !== id) : [...saved.dropped, id];
      save();
      draw();
      updateAverage();
      if (saved.revealed.includes("pond-md-need-missing")) hooks["pond-md-need-missing"]();
    });
    draw();
  });
  updateAverage();
  hooks["pond-md-need-missing"] = () => {
    updateAverage();
    const d = new Set(saved.dropped);
    const right = average(dropRows.filter(tr => tr.cells[0].textContent.trim() !== "M-03"));
    let verdict;
    if (d.size === 1 && d.has("M-03")) verdict = "✓ You dropped exactly M-03.";
    else if (d.has("M-04")) verdict = "You dropped M-04, a real measurement of 99 ppm.";
    else if (!d.has("M-03")) verdict = "You kept M-03, which was never analyzed.";
    else verdict = "You dropped more than M-03.";
    dropStatus.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "<br>");
    dropStatus.append(`${verdict} With only M-03 dropped, the average is ${right} ppm.`);
  };

  // 1.5 Surface samples above 400 ppm
  document.querySelectorAll("#pond-md-surface button").forEach(btn => {
    btn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(saved.surface.includes(btn.dataset.id)));
    btn.addEventListener("click", () => {
      const on = btn.getAttribute("aria-pressed") !== "true";
      btn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(on));
      saved.surface = on ? [...saved.surface, btn.dataset.id] : saved.surface.filter(x => x !== btn.dataset.id);
      save();
      if (saved.revealed.includes("pond-md-need-dry")) hooks["pond-md-need-dry"]();
    });
  });
  hooks["pond-md-need-dry"] = () => {
    const out = document.getElementById("pond-md-surface-out");
    const mine = [...saved.surface].sort().join(", ");
    out.innerHTML = `<p class="pond-pad-take"></p>`;
    out.firstChild.textContent = mine === "M-01, M-06"
      ? "✓ You picked M-01 and M-06. Did you know about the water content, or was it a lucky guess?"
      : `You picked: ${mine || "none"}. In dry soil, M-01 and M-06 are above 400 ppm.`;
  };

  // Restore activities revealed on an earlier visit (after the hooks exist)
  Pond.restore(state, needs);

  // ---------- Response summary (shared builder in scripts/response-summary.js) ----------

  const limitText = v => v > 400 ? "**above** the 400 ppm limit" : "below the 400 ppm limit";
  const csv = document.querySelector("#quarto-document-content pre, main pre");

  PondSummary.attach({
    button: document.getElementById("pond-md-download"),
    filename: "metadata-response-summary.md",
    title: "Metadata for Reuse",
    idea: "A data file is not necessarily usable just because it opens.",
    intro: csv ? ["## The file I was given\n\n```\n" + csv.textContent.trim() + "\n```"] : [],
    next: { text: "Data Quality and Provenance", href: "../data-quality/index.html" },
    handlers: [
      { selector: ".pond-md-need", md: el => Pond.needMd(needs.find(n => n.bank === el)) },
      { selector: "#pond-md-depth", md: el => {
          const v = parseFloat(el.value);
          return Number.isNaN(v) ? "**My depth for M-02:** *not answered.* It's 6 inches, or 0.15 m."
            : `**My depth for M-02:** ${v} m. ${depthMessage(v)}`;
        } },
      { selector: "#pond-md-drop", md: () => {
          const kept = dropRows.filter(tr => !saved.dropped.includes(tr.cells[0].textContent.trim()));
          const right = average(dropRows.filter(tr => tr.cells[0].textContent.trim() !== "M-03"));
          const mine = kept.length ? `${average(kept)} ppm, ${limitText(average(kept))}` : "no rows left";
          return `**Rows I dropped:** ${saved.dropped.length ? [...saved.dropped].sort().join(", ") : "none"}.  \n` +
            `Raw average: ${average(dropRows)} ppm. My cleaned average: ${mine}. ` +
            `Correctly cleaned (M-03 only): ${right} ppm, ${limitText(right)}.`;
        } },
      { selector: "#pond-md-surface", md: () =>
          `**Surface samples I thought were above 400 ppm:** ${[...saved.surface].sort().join(", ") || "none"}. In dry soil, it's M-01 and M-06.` },
      { selector: ".pond-md-recap", md: el => PondSummary.elementMd(el.querySelector("table")) }
    ]
  });
});
</script>
```
